newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says U.S. will not abandon Rwanda refugees.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says U.S. will not abandon Rwanda refugees.

text.p: The United States remains prepared to contribute troops to a Zaire relief mission despite encouraging signs Rwandan refugees have begun heading home, President Bill Clinton said on Friday.
"The world's most powerful nation must not turn its back on so many desperate people and so many innocent children," Clinton said at a White House news conference.

"The mission Canada proposes to lead, and that I believe America should take part in, would provide security for civilian relief agencies to deliver the aid these people must have and to help the refugees who so desire to return home to Rwanda," he said.

Washington announced earlier this week it had agreed tentatively to send 1,000 troops to Goma, Zaire, to secure the airport and set up a protected corridor so refugees can return to Rwanda. Another 3,000 U.S. troops or so would provide support from neighbouring countries.
The U.S. commitment was conditioned on getting assurances the scope and duration of the humanitarian relief mission would be specific and limited, among other demands.

Reports of a sudden mass movement of Rwandan refugees toward home raised questions of whether this might eliminate the need for an international relief mission, but Clinton said it would be premature to draw any such conclusion.
"It's a hopeful sign but that's about all I can say right now," he said of the refugee movement reports.

He promised U.S. troops would be authorised to defend themselves with firepower if the United States joins a proposed Canadian-led international force to provide security for civilian relief agencies trying to help the refugees.

He said such rules of engagement were essential to any humanitarian military mission, and referred to what he called the successful international mission to the former Yugoslavia as evidence that such rules work.
He said it was unlikely, however, that any U.S. or international forces would face conditions so hostile that they would have to "shoot our way in."

"We obviously understand if you've got a lot of people around there with guns, somebody might shoot at you, and you would have to be able to shoot back," Clinton said. "But that's different from having an official policy that if this international mission goes in, they're going to be considered an invading force and be subject to attack from the minute that the airplane lands."

Defence Secretary William Perry, who also attended the news conference, said the United States requires "cooperation from the governments (of Zaire and Rwanda), but we did not want to make forced landings at the airfield."
"On the other hand, the guerrilla forces that are located in that area, whatever they tell us, we want acquiescence, but we do not expect to have any formal agreement from them," Perry said.
At the same news conference, Clinton unveiled plans to extend the U.S. presence in the former Yugoslavia, prompting sceptical comment from political critics.

"Troops should be committed as a last resort, not a first resort," Senator Dan Coats, an Indiana Republican, said on CNN. "As we've learned in Bosnia, once there, it's very, very difficult to get them out."
